Flash attributes distinguish success, not-found, and failure messages; these outcomes do not produce 204, 404, or controller 500. Missing/invalid Basic credentials: 401.
Photo Album / PhotoFileController.servePhotoGET/photo/{id}String path ID; optional browser _t cache-busting query is not bound or used by the controller200 ResponseEntity backed by ByteArrayResource, with stored MIME type. Blank ID reaching the handler, absent photo, or null/empty bytes: empty 404. Caught lookup/content-type/resource preparation exception: empty 500.

Upload contract details: files are processed sequentially, with a separate transactional service invocation per file; the request is not an all-or-nothing batch. success is true only when at least one saved photo was successfully read back and added to uploadedPhotos. A successful service result whose read-back is empty is omitted from both lists. A thrown read-back exception interrupts processing rather than returning the accumulated result. Service-reported rejections remain entries in failedUploads with HTTP 200; there is no controller-level @Valid request DTO producing a uniform validation 400. Multipart parser limits are 10 MB per file and 50 MB per request; the controller's MultipartException handler maps exceptions reaching it to the generic 400 response, not an explicit 413 contract. Container/filter-level rejection behavior is not customized. The configured file-count setting is not consumed by the upload controller or service, so it is not an enforced count contract. See business-workflows.md for individual validation rules.

Image response headers: Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, private, Pragma: no-cache, Expires: 0, plus X-Photo-ID, X-Photo-Name, and X-Photo-Size. The controller adds no download Content-Disposition. These headers are added on the successful response, not on its empty error responses.

Framework surface: static resources include /css/site.css and /js/upload.js; they are not additional annotated business endpoints. Boot's default /error handling is framework-provided, not a custom controller contract. GET mappings also receive normal Spring MVC HEAD support, and OPTIONS/method mismatch handling is framework-managed; no explicit PUT, PATCH, DELETE, or custom OPTIONS routes exist. A missing path segment does not invoke a controller's blank-ID branch.

Communication Patterns

  • Synchronous boundary and internal calls: the browser fetches gallery/detail HTML and image bytes, uploads through same-origin fetch('/upload'), and deletes with a normal POST form. Controllers call PhotoServiceImpl directly; it calls PhotoRepository and Oracle through JDBC/JPA. These are not separately deployed REST services. The detail page assembles the current photo and previous/next IDs from local service calls, not gateway composition.
  • External browser resources: templates load Bootstrap CSS and JavaScript from cdn.jsdelivr.net over HTTPS. This is browser-to-CDN traffic, not backend service discovery or a backend REST dependency; no application-defined CDN fallback is present.
  • No asynchronous service contract: browser async/await still uses request/response HTTP. No broker, queue, event publication, gRPC, backend HTTP client, scheduled messaging, or pub/sub implementation was found.
  • Resilience and timeouts: no explicit retries, circuit breaker, bulkhead, fallback library, or application HTTP/JDBC/query timeout value is configured. Do not infer a timeout of zero or infinite from this absence; runtime/library defaults apply. Browser upload uses one fetch attempt, without a timeout/abort or retry policy. Compose's process restart policy is not a request retry. Application fallbacks are the empty gallery, redirect-on-detail/delete failure, upload failure entries where caught, and photo-byte 404/500 responses described above. Transaction completion errors can escape the upload service's internal catches.
  • Discovery, gateway, and balancing: no Eureka/Consul, logical-service registry, API gateway, gateway response merging, or client-side load balancer. The database uses a configured JDBC address, resolving oracle-db in Compose and defaulting to localhost outside Compose; this is container name resolution rather than application service registration.
  • Availability dependency: Compose starts the application after the database is healthy; database connectivity and externally supplied database/admin credentials are startup dependencies. There is no separate application readiness route. Full startup/probe and environment configuration belongs in configuration-inventory.md.
  • Authentication and authorization: Spring Security enables HTTP Basic and stateless security session management. Only POST /upload and POST /detail/*/delete require an authenticated principal; other requests are explicitly permitted by the filter chain, subject to route matching. The sole configured in-memory user has role ADMIN and a BCrypt-encoded password from external configuration, but the endpoint rule is authenticated(), not hasRole("ADMIN"); there is no per-photo ownership check, method-security annotation, JWT, or OAuth2 integration. Missing/invalid credentials for protected requests normally produce 401 with a Basic challenge; the JSON upload error envelope is not a security error format. Default Spring Basic handling can suppress the challenge header for requests marked X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest; the supplied fetch does not set that header. Supplying invalid Basic credentials can also cause authentication failure on an otherwise public route.
  • Browser/authentication interaction: upload JavaScript does not explicitly construct an Authorization header or provide a sign-in flow; a client must supply valid Basic credentials or rely on browser-managed credentials. Delete flash messages may use MVC flash/session infrastructure; stateless Spring Security does not establish that the entire MVC application is session-free.
  • CSRF, CORS, and transport: CSRF is explicitly disabled, so protected POSTs do not require a CSRF token. No custom CORS policy is configured. Application HTTPS/TLS, HTTPS enforcement, reverse-proxy TLS termination, and database TLS are not configured in the inspected source/deployment files; the application exposes HTTP on 8080. HTTPS CDN URLs do not secure the application's Basic-auth traffic. Spring Security's default headers are not a configured TLS listener.

Service Communication Sequence

Primary write flow: authenticated multipart upload, with per-file results and subsequent public image retrieval. Solid arrows are synchronous calls; dashed arrows are responses, not broker messages. No gateway, retry, or circuit breaker exists to depict.

The 200 upload response assumes no uncaught service/transaction/read-back exception; such failures instead escape to framework error handling, potentially 500. An empty read-back is omitted rather than converted into a per-file failure. Startup Dependency Chain

  1. Compose launch → required environment inputs: Compose interpolates ORACLE_PASSWORD, APP_USER_PASSWORD, and APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD with required/nonempty checks before starting services.
  2. oracle-db → Oracle image initialization/startup: the image receives ORACLE_PWD, APP_USER, APP_USER_PASSWORD, and ORACLE_CHARACTERSET; the startup directory mount supplies 01-create-user.sh, 02-verify-user.sql, create-user.sh, and healthcheck.sql. Script discovery/execution is image-managed, not explicitly orchestrated by Compose.
  3. Schema scripts → Oracle SQL listener: both shell scripts use SQL*Plus as SYSTEM with ENV ORACLE_PWD against //localhost:1521/XE. 01-create-user.sh has no explicit wait loop; create-user.sh sleeps 30 seconds. Both use set -euo pipefail and shell required-variable checks. The verification SQL checks fixed username PHOTOALBUM, so its diagnostic target does not track an overridden APP_USER.
  4. Database healthy → successful application-user SQL query: Compose pipes SELECT 1 FROM DUAL; to SQLPlus using container ENV APP_USER / APP_USER_PASSWORD. $${...} escaping defers expansion to the container shell. Timing is interval: 30s, timeout: 10s, retries: 15, start_period: 180s; the grace period and retry timing are not an application startup timeout. The checked-in command relies on SQLPlus exit status and has no WHENEVER SQLERROR EXIT directive.
  5. photoalbum-java-app → waits for → oracle-db: Compose depends_on uses condition: service_healthy, then launches the Java entrypoint. There is no dockerize wait, custom database retry configuration, separate config/discovery service, or application readiness probe. This dependency gates initial startup; it is not ongoing database-availability enforcement.

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

  1. Operator copies .env.example to ignored .env and replaces placeholders with unique private values, or supplies equivalent shell variables. Any illustrative password assignment is represented only as APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD=[MASKED], APP_USER_PASSWORD=[MASKED], or ORACLE_PASSWORD=[MASKED].
  2. Compose validates required secret inputs and injects them as plain container environment variables. .env is an interpolation source, not an automatic blanket export to all containers.
  3. Oracle receives its administrative credential through ORACLE_PWD. Initialization connects as SYSTEM, creates the configured application user when absent, and applies schema-scoped grants; the primary script does not grant DBA. The scripts do not update an existing user's password, so changing environment values alone does not rotate persisted database credentials.
  4. The application receives the same schema credential through SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD, plus APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD. Spring resolves these into the datasource and admin configuration. The administrator is constructed in memory with a BCrypt password encoder; this does not encrypt environment-variable storage.
  5. The test profile instead supplies its own test credential fixture and H2 password setting, both [MASKED] here. No deployment pipeline secret retrieval or automatic secret rotation workflow is configured in the examined deployment sources.

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album lets visitors browse uploaded photos, inspect their metadata, and navigate between images. Authenticated users can add photos in batches and permanently delete individual photos.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
PhotoPhotoService / Photo ManagementAn individually uploaded image, its original content, and information used for gallery and detail presentation. The only persisted business entity and natural aggregate boundary.Appears in the shared gallery; older and newer photos are located by upload time rather than explicit relationships. No owner or album entity exists.
UploadResultPhotoService / Upload ProcessingTransient per-file outcome identifying an accepted photo or explaining rejection. Not a persisted entity or independent aggregate.A successful result references a Photo; the controller combines results into batch feedback.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:19-91, model/UploadResult.java:6-14, and service/PhotoService.java:13-54 (Java paths below are relative to src/main/java/com/photoalbum/ unless otherwise stated).

Service-to-Domain Mapping

This is one application, not a set of independently deployed domain services. The rows below describe internal responsibilities, not microservices.

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
PhotoService / PhotoServiceImplPhoto Management and Upload ProcessingPhoto aggregate; creates UploadResult outcomesPhotoRepository and the configured database; image-header inspection

PhotoRepository provides the shared persistence boundary; it is not another business service. The database is the source of truth for both image bytes and metadata. All controller-to-service exchanges are local calls; there are no domain events, remote domain services, gateway aggregation, or cross-context foreign keys in the inspected application.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload a Batch and Update the Visible Gallery

  1. On the gallery page, a visitor selects multiple files or drops them into the upload area. Selection immediately invokes the upload JavaScript; there is no separate upload button or authentication form.
  2. JavaScript applies Browser upload eligibility, collects eligible files into one multipart request, and displays an uploading indicator. Ineligible files are not submitted.
  3. The request enters through POST /upload. Mutation authorization must pass before controller processing. The controller applies Batch presence and processes files sequentially through PhotoService.
  4. Each service invocation applies Server upload eligibility and Image inspection, reads the bytes, constructs a Photo, and saves bytes and metadata together. A new Photo receives an identifier and upload time under Photo identity and lifecycle.
  5. The service returns a per-file UploadResult. For each reported success, the controller performs a separate lookup and constructs display metadata. Rejections become filename/error entries. There is no transaction spanning the whole batch.
  6. An ordinarily processed batch returns HTTP 200 with successful metadata and failures; its success flag is true only when the successful metadata list is nonempty. Missing batch input takes the controller's HTTP 400 branch. Successful files remain saved even when other files fail.
  7. JavaScript prepends returned photo cards without reloading, removing the empty-gallery message or creating a gallery container if needed. Each card causes a separate image-content request. Cards are inserted one at a time at the beginning, reversing response order visually; a later gallery reload applies database ordering.
  8. Success feedback automatically hides after five seconds. Server per-file failures can be displayed alongside successes. Non-2xx responses and network/JSON errors produce generic messages, not the server's detailed error body.

Actual presentation caveat: client rejections call showErrors, but that function does not reveal the initially hidden feedback container. If the same selection contains eligible files, starting their upload hides the rejection list. Thus the intended client feedback is not reliably visible. JavaScript also does not explicitly supply credentials or offer login; authentication must be satisfied by the request/browser context.

Reporting gap: if the post-save lookup returns empty, the saved photo is omitted from both lists. If that lookup or a transaction commit throws, it can terminate the request rather than produce a per-file failure, while earlier committed uploads remain stored.

Evidence: controller/HomeController.java:54-106, service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:81-185, model/Photo.java:78-91, src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:48-159,205-220, src/main/resources/templates/index.html:48-77.

Workflow 2: Browse the Shared Gallery and Display Image Content

  1. GET / calls PhotoService to retrieve the gallery using Gallery ordering. The template renders filenames, upload times, sizes, and available dimensions, with links to details.
  2. If retrieval fails, the controller logs the error and substitutes an empty list. The same “No photos yet” prompt is shown for both genuine emptiness and a database failure; no outage warning distinguishes them.
  3. Gallery image elements independently request GET /photo/{id}. PhotoFileController looks up the Photo and applies Image availability.
  4. Available bytes are served directly from the database with the stored MIME type. There is no thumbnail-generation workflow: gallery cards and detail pages request the same original content.
  5. Missing data returns 404; unexpected lookup or response-construction errors return 500. There is no implemented placeholder-image fallback.
  6. Images are served with no-cache/no-store response headers. Dynamically added cards also append a timestamp to image URLs; ordinary server-rendered gallery images do not use the timestamp model attribute.

Evidence: controller/HomeController.java:38-50, controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-86, repository/PhotoRepository.java:23-29, src/main/resources/templates/index.html:81-113, src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:161-202.

Workflow 3: Inspect a Photo and Navigate to Adjacent Uploads

  1. GET /detail/{id} checks Detail availability and looks up the selected Photo.
  2. For an existing Photo, the controller independently requests older and newer candidates using Temporal navigation. It adds the first candidate's identifier in each direction to the view.
  3. The detail template presents the original image, filename, upload time, formatted size, MIME type, and dimensions when present. It shows navigation buttons only when candidate identifiers exist.
  4. The image itself is retrieved through the independent content-delivery workflow, so rendered metadata does not guarantee the subsequent image request succeeds.
  5. Invalid/missing photos or exceptions, including navigation-query failures, redirect to the gallery. Although the template contains a “Photo not found” branch, this controller does not render it for a missing record.

Evidence: controller/DetailController.java:32-58, service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:213-230, repository/PhotoRepository.java:37-62, src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:32-38,62-132.

Workflow 4: Delete a Photo and Return to the Gallery

  1. The detail template offers a delete form. Browser confirmation cancels submission if declined; this is a UI safeguard, not a server-side approval rule.
  2. Confirmed submission enters POST /detail/{id}/delete, subject to Mutation authorization.
  3. PhotoService looks up the Photo. Absence returns false; presence triggers deletion of the single database entity, including its stored image content.
  4. The controller redirects to the gallery in every handled outcome. It supplies a success flash message for deletion, “Photo not found” for absence, or a generic failure flash message after an exception; the gallery template renders these messages.
  5. Deletion is permanent at the application level. There is no recycle bin, soft-delete state, filesystem cleanup, or compensating operation.

Evidence: src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50-59, controller/DetailController.java:64-78, service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:190-209, src/main/resources/templates/index.html:37-46.

Workflow 5: Update Capability and Startup State

No photo-update workflow is implemented. There is no controller entry point, service operation, edit form, or JavaScript action for renaming, replacing image bytes, or editing metadata. Entity setters and the generic repository's persistence capabilities do not constitute an exposed business workflow. The visible “update” after uploading is a gallery DOM change, not mutation of an existing Photo.

Startup launches the application without a custom business initializer, seed process, scheduler, batch command, or event listener in the inspected source. However, both checked-in application profiles set spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=create; schema recreation on startup can discard existing photo state. Persistent storage should not be interpreted as an application guarantee that photos survive restarts under this configuration.

Evidence: service/PhotoService.java:13-54, the three controllers cited above, src/main/resources/templates/index.html, src/main/resources/templates/detail.html, src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js, PhotoAlbumApplication.java:9-14, src/main/resources/application.properties:17-30, src/main/resources/application-docker.properties:13-27.

Cross-Service Data Flows

There are no cross-service business calls or circuit breakers to trace. Within the application:

  • Upload response composition: browser files → HomeController → one PhotoService transaction per file → shared database; successful identifiers → separate PhotoService lookups → metadata response → new browser cards. Binary content is not included in this response.
  • Detail composition: selected identifier → Photo lookup → separate older/newer queries using its upload time → template with photo information and navigation identifiers. These reads are not enclosed in a single controller-level transaction/snapshot.
  • Content composition: a card/detail page supplies the photo identifier in an image URL; an independent browser request retrieves the bytes from the same database. There is no join with an external image store.
  • Degradation: gallery lookup failure looks like an empty gallery; detail or navigation failure redirects home; content absence produces 404 and content exceptions produce 500. Upload and deletion failures use the outcomes described above, not a fallback service or queue.

Filesystem/database consistency: application code stores original image bytes and metadata in the same Photo record. There is no application-managed upload directory, filename-to-path mapping, file move, or separate durable filesystem write/delete to coordinate with database transactions. Request buffering and image-library temporary caching, if used by the runtime, are not business photo storage. Database-content consistency still has limits: nullable image content and permissive inspection mean a listed Photo need not have renderable bytes; post-upload reads and independent image requests can observe later deletion.

Actual versus intended documentation: README.md:27-36 describes the original database-backed photo store and a future PostgreSQL/managed-identity/Azure deployment. The inspected implementation still uses database BLOB photo storage and database-specific navigation queries; those workshop migration goals are not implemented business flows. Read access is public and mutation access uses application HTTP Basic authentication, not per-photo ownership or a passwordless end-user flow.

sequenceDiagram participant U as "Visitor" participant B as "Gallery browser" participant C as "Upload controller and access gate" participant S as "Photo service" participant P as "Photo aggregate" participant D as "Photo database" U->>B: Select or drop photos B->>B: Apply browser upload eligibility B->>C: Submit eligible files alt Authentication fails C-->>B: Reject mutation request B-->>U: Generic upload failure else Authentication succeeds loop Each submitted file C->>S: Process photo upload S->>S: Apply server eligibility and image inspection alt Rejected or file read fails S-->>C: Per-file rejection reason else Eligible file S->>P: Create photo with content and metadata S->>D: Save photo in per-file transaction alt Save and commit succeed S-->>C: Successful photo identifier C->>S: Retrieve saved photo for gallery metadata S->>D: Find photo by identifier D-->>S: Photo or absence S-->>C: Metadata when present else Save fails S-->>C: Failure result or propagated commit error Note over C,D: Commit errors can abort request after earlier files persist end end end Note over C,B: Ordinary completion aggregates successes and failures C-->>B: Batch outcome if processing completes B->>B: Prepend successful cards and request image content B-->>U: Gallery additions and upload feedback end

Business Rules & Decision Logic

Validation and Eligibility

Named ruleActual decision and consequenceEvidence
Browser upload eligibilityAccepts reported file types image/jpeg, image/png, image/gif, image/webp; rejects sizes greater than 10 × 1024 × 1024 bytes. Exactly the limit is allowed. Zero-byte files are not explicitly rejected here. File-picker accept is only a selection hint.src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:60-88; templates/index.html:63 under resources
Batch presenceController returns HTTP 400 for a null/empty list; its MultipartException handler also returns HTTP 400 with “No files provided,” even when the multipart error has a different cause. Required-parameter binding may reject missing input before the explicit branch.controller/HomeController.java:58-67,100-106
Server upload eligibilityLowercases reported content type for membership in the configured allowed list; rejects a size above 10,485,760 bytes or a nonpositive size. A null content type causes the outer generic-error branch, not a specific MIME rejection. Submitted MIME is retained for storage; filename extension is not checked.service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:85-118,154-160,178-182; src/main/resources/application.properties:23-30
Image inspectionReads image dimensions from the first available image reader's header; rejects a width × height product greater than 40,000,000. It does not fully decode, transcode, or verify declared MIME against detected content. No reader means acceptance without dimensions. IOException means rejection; other inspection exceptions are logged and processing continues without guaranteed dimensions. Thus allowed MIME alone does not prove a valid/renderable image, and WebP dimensions depend on available readers.service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:33-34,111-152
Entity constraintsDeclares nonblank original filename (maximum 255 characters), nonnull positive file size, nonblank MIME (maximum 50 characters), and nonnull upload time. Image bytes are nullable; dimensions have no positivity annotations. These are entity/persistence constraints, not an explicit controller @Valid request-validation step, so persistence/provider enforcement and commit timing determine their failure path.model/Photo.java:28-75; controller/HomeController.java:58; service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:164-182
Batch capacityMultipart configuration caps each file at 10MB and the request at 50MB. The configured app.file-upload.max-files-per-upload=10 is not read/enforced by the service or browser; there is no implemented ten-photo count check.src/main/resources/application.properties:23-30; src/main/resources/application-docker.properties:19-27; service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:36-47; controller/HomeController.java:69-91

Availability, Ordering, and Lifecycle

  • Photo identity and lifecycle: construction generates a UUID and local upload timestamp. A photo progresses from submitted bytes to a persisted Photo or a rejection, then can be read or permanently deleted. There is no explicit status field, moderation/approval state, or update transition. No filename uniqueness or content deduplication rule exists; repeated uploads create distinct photos. (model/Photo.java:78-91; service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:154-170,190-205.)
  • Gallery ordering: all photos are retrieved newest-first, without pagination or a secondary tie-breaker; the gallery query substitutes a generic MIME value for null stored MIME. That query substitution is not an upload validation rule or a guaranteed fallback on direct identifier lookup. (repository/PhotoRepository.java:23-29.)
  • Temporal navigation: previous chooses the first older photo from a descending-time query capped at ten returned candidates. Next chooses the first newer photo in ascending order, additionally excluding uploads after database SYSDATE. Comparisons are strict, so photos with equal timestamps are not linked by these queries; there is no wraparound. Application-local timestamps and database time may differ. (repository/PhotoRepository.java:37-62; service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:217-230.)
  • Detail availability: blank identifiers, absent records, or lookup/navigation exceptions redirect to the gallery. Image availability: blank identifiers, missing records, or null/empty bytes return 404; unexpected exceptions, including invalid stored media type parsing, return 500. A metadata record can therefore be visible while its image fails. (controller/DetailController.java:32-58; controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-86.)
  • Computed display values: dimensions are optional header-derived values; displayed dates and human-readable sizes are presentation calculations. Gallery sizes are rounded KB; detail sizes switch between bytes, KB, and MB. No pricing, quotas per user, relationship-maintenance rules, or business totals are implemented. (src/main/resources/templates/index.html:101-107; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:108-130; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:162-197.)

Transactions, Consistency, and Failures

  • PhotoServiceImpl has class-level transactions; retrieval and navigation methods declare read-only transactions. Each controller-invoked upload/delete is its own service boundary. Batch processing, subsequent metadata lookups, and detail composition are not one atomic operation. (service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:27-29,52-74,190-229; controller/HomeController.java:69-91.)
  • Image content and its metadata are saved/deleted together as one database entity, with no dual-write filesystem consistency problem. There is no explicit flush before forming an upload success result, and an exception during transaction completion can escape the method's catch blocks. Catching save errors does not guarantee transaction recovery; the transaction may already require rollback. Deletion errors are wrapped as runtime exceptions and handled by the controller. (service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:154-184,190-209.)
  • There is no implemented retry, outbox, saga, compensating delete for upload-reporting failures, or reconciliation job. Concurrent reads/deletes can make a page or successful upload response stale. Schema recreation at startup is a separate durability risk, not a photo lifecycle rule. (src/main/resources/application.properties:19; src/main/resources/application-docker.properties:15.)

Authorization and Audit

  • Mutation authorization: the security filter requires authentication for upload and deletion POSTs using stateless HTTP Basic. It creates one configured in-memory administrator with ADMIN role, but these request matchers require only authentication, not an explicit role test. Other requests are permitted. There is no photo ownership field or per-resource authorization check; an authenticated caller can delete any photo. CSRF protection is disabled. Templates expose upload and delete controls without role-aware hiding. (config/SecurityConfig.java:33-59; gallery/detail templates.)
  • Successful uploads/deletions, rejections, and exceptions are logged, but there is no persisted audit trail, recorded acting user, edit history, or domain-event history. Content delivery also logs filenames, sizes, and a short byte prefix for debugging; that is not an access-audit model. (service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:90-100,171-180,195-208; controller/PhotoFileController.java:45-72.)

This document describes source-observed behavior; README workshop goals, comments, configured-but-unused settings, and template-only branches are not treated as implemented guarantees. No application execution or tests were performed for this source-based assessment.

Version & Compatibility Risks

Spring Boot 3.5.0 is the initial 3.5 release rather than a later maintenance patch; review supported patch levels before modernization. Commons IO 2.14.0 is independently pinned and needs its own maintenance review. Preserve Java 21 and the Spring Boot 3 Jakarta-era compatibility baseline when changing framework components; validate the Oracle driver against the target JDK and database rather than inferring compatibility from the ojdbc8 artifact name. Build metadata alone does not establish current end-of-life status or known vulnerability exposure.

Optional devtools remains a direct compile dependency but is not propagated automatically to downstream consumers; optionality does not itself mean exclusion from every packaged artifact.
  • The JSON starter is a JSON-support dependency, not an image-processing library, despite the local POM comment. Its possible overlap with the web starter cannot be treated as a resolved transitive relationship from the local declaration alone.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The data layer contains one Jakarta Persistence entity, Photo, accessed through Spring Data JPA/Hibernate. Oracle stores photo metadata and binary content together; the test profile substitutes an in-memory H2 database.

  • Test fidelity: The sole test activates test and loads the application context; it does not execute repository queries or verify Oracle/H2 behavioral equivalence (src/test/java/com/photoalbum/PhotoAlbumApplicationTests.java:7-14). The entity declares a nonunique index on uploaded_at (Photo.java:16-18), but no optimistic-lock @Version, entity relationships, cascade/orphan-removal rules, or explicit lazy loading for the LOB. UUID and timestamp initialization occurs in the constructor (Photo.java:78-91). UploadResult is a transient result object, not an entity (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/UploadResult.java:6-10).

Binary/metadata consistency: The upload service puts bytes and their metadata into the same entity/save operation, avoiding a separate database-to-filesystem commit boundary (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:111-176). Filename, file size, and MIME type come from the multipart object; size is not recomputed from the stored byte array and MIME type is not derived from the image reader. Dimensions come from image headers when a reader is available; unsupported/unreadable dimension extraction can leave them null. The stored bytes are not re-encoded or stripped of embedded metadata. No checksum, database rule tying file_size to LOB length, or automatic reconciliation is present in the inspected mapping/service. Because the LOB column is nullable, metadata-only rows are permitted by the mapping; binary serving explicitly treats null/empty data as unavailable (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:53-62).

The test configuration retains an upload-directory setting, but the current service does not inject/use it. A tracked image exists under src/main/resources/static/uploads/; no inspected persistence code links it to photos or imports it as seed data. It should not be interpreted as a second active photo store.

Transactions: PhotoServiceImpl has class-level Spring @Transactional; its four read operations override this with read-only transactions (PhotoServiceImpl.java:27-28,52-75,215-230). Upload and deletion use the default write transaction. Deletion loads and removes the entity within that service transaction; failures are rethrown as runtime exceptions (PhotoServiceImpl.java:190-209). No distributed transaction, explicit isolation/locking, or custom propagation is configured.

Upload catches save failures and returns a failed result rather than propagating them (PhotoServiceImpl.java:164-184). This does not guarantee clean recovery: a repository failure may already mark the transaction rollback-only, and flush/commit failures can occur after the method body returns through the transaction interceptor. Success is set after save, not after an explicit flush. Multiple uploads are separate externally invoked service transactions, not one atomic batch; the controller loop itself has no transaction annotation (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:58-91).

Key Repository Methods

Photo AlbumPhotoRepository extends JpaRepositoryList findAllOrderByUploadedAtDesc()Native SQL returns all rows, newest first, including LOB bytes; uses Oracle NVL to substitute a MIME value in the query result
Photo AlbumPhotoRepositoryList findPhotosUploadedBefore(LocalDateTime uploadedAt)Bound timestamp parameter; strictly older rows ordered descending, limited to 10 by Oracle ROWNUM in an outer query

Source: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:15-62. All three custom methods use native @Query SQL rather than derived queries. Standard CRUD is inherited from JpaRepository and is not repeated in the table; the service uses inherited persistence operations for lookup, saving, and deletion. No custom bulk aggregation query, stored-procedure call, named query, or separate JDBC mapper was found.

Persistence implications:

  • These are entity queries containing photo_data, not metadata-only projections. The gallery query is unbounded, and the newer-photo query can load many LOBs even though the service takes only the first returned entity (PhotoServiceImpl.java:217-229).
  • Timestamp comparisons are strict and ordering has no ID tie-breaker. Equal-timestamp photos are not reachable through these before/after queries; deterministic ordering among timestamp ties is not specified.
  • Newer-photo selection compares application-generated local timestamps with the database server clock. Future-dated records are excluded until database time catches up.
  • NVL supplies a read-time fallback; it does not repair the stored MIME value or change the mapping's non-null requirement.

Data Ownership Boundaries

The inspected project has one persistence-owning application module and one application database connection per active configuration. It is not a database-per-microservice topology: metadata and image content share the photos table and transaction boundary. H2 is an alternative test store, not a replica, read model, or additional production persistence tier.

Controllers obtain data through PhotoService, whose implementation accesses PhotoRepository; no cross-service REST data retrieval, shared-database access by another service, federation, or gateway aggregation is present in the inspected source. The same entity/repository serves reads and writes, with no CQRS split or event-driven synchronization. No owner/user/tenant foreign key or row-level ownership partition is modeled.

No encryption-at-rest setting or application-level encrypted LOB mapping was found; Oracle infrastructure encryption cannot be confirmed from these files. Logging includes original filenames and photo IDs during upload and serving, and binary serving logs up to the first ten stored bytes without redaction (PhotoServiceImpl.java:171-179; PhotoFileController.java:53-72).
